newsitem.title: GERMANY: "English Patient" tipped for Berlin festival prize.
newsitem.headline: "English Patient" tipped for Berlin festival prize.

text.p: Critics are tipping the film "The English Patient" by a relatively unknown British director, Anthony Minghella, to clinch the the "Golden Bear" prize for best film at the 47th Berlin film festival on Monday.

But the controversial film "The People vs Larry Flynt" by Czech director Milos Forman about the Hustler magazine publisher and director Yim Ho's "Kitchen" based on a Japanese novel about a young girl growing up in Hong Kong are also hot contenders.
"These are the films the critics have been most keen on," said a festival spokeswoman who asked not to be named. But, she added, in previous years there have been surprise winners too.

Festival organiser Moritz de Hadeln will announce the ten-member jury's decision later on Monday at a news conference. He will award the prizes in a glittering evening ceremony at Berlin's Zoo Palast cinema.

With relatively few big names represented at the festival this year, possibly because Europe's top film festival at Cannes will mark its 50th anniversary in May, less well-known film-makers have come under the spotlight.

Minghella, 43, who lectured at Britain's Hull University before taking up film-making in 1992, said he was stunned by the success of "The English Patient" after it won 12 Academy Award nominations for best picture in Los Angeles this month.

He said he started the project to film the romantic war-time epic set in Italy and Africa and based on a complex novel by Canadian Michael Ondaatje four years ago, but it took a long time to convince Hollywood studios to back him.

French star Juliet Binoche, who plays a French-Canadian nurse who helps a man suffering from amnesia in Minghella's film, and Woody Harrelson, who plays pornographer Flynt, were hotly tipped for the "Silver Bear" awards for best performances.

The Flynt film, which won two Oscar nominations this month, depicts the tumultuous life of publisher Larry Flynt, a school drop-out who ran strip clubs in Ohio before launching his successful magazine Hustler in 1973.

In France Roman Catholics tried unsuccessfully to ban its poster, showing Harrelson, arms outstretched as if on a cross, wearing only briefs made of the Stars and Stripes flag, against a backdrop of a woman's bikini-clad loins.
The poster was rejected by the Motion Picture Association of America. In Australia and Switzerland it was branded as offensive and sacriligious by the Catholic Church.
The rest of the 25 films in the competition, though liked, were not really seen as prize material, the spokeswoman said.
A big budget German-Danish co-production "Smilla's Sense of Snow" which opened the festival was tipped as an early favourite but failed to receive enthusiastic reviews.

Critics saw "The Crucible", based on the play of the same title by Arthur Miller and dealing with witchhunts among early settlers in New England starring Daniel Day-Lewis, as a solid but unexciting costume drama.

They dubbed Australian director Baz Luhrmann's "William Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet" a "rock 'n roll" version of the famous love story. It was popular but possibly "too camp" to win one of prestigious awards, the spokeswoman said.
Although German films have recently made a big comeback, the only pure German competition entry "Life is a Construction Site", although popular, was unlikely to be in the running.
A Taiwan film "The River" by director Tsai Ming-Liang about urban alienation in Tapei has been tipped by some critics as a hot favourite for an award, if not the Golden Bear, for best film.
